title: Our Environment
description: Grade 10 Biology: ecosystems and their components, food chains, food webs and trophic levels, flow of energy (the 10% law), ozone depletion and waste management.

topics.title: Ecosystem: Components and Food Chains
topics.concept:
An ecosystem is a self-contained unit in which living organisms interact with one another and with their non-living surroundings. A forest, a pond, a lake and a crop field are examples. An ecosystem has two kinds of components:

  • Biotic (living) components — all the living organisms, grouped by how they obtain food: producers (green plants, which make food), consumers (animals, which eat others) and decomposers.
  • Abiotic (non-living) components — physical factors such as sunlight, temperature, air, water and soil.

Consumers are further classified by what they eat: herbivores (primary consumers, eat plants), carnivores (secondary/tertiary consumers, eat other animals) and omnivores (eat both). Decomposers — bacteria and fungi — break down dead plants and animals and return the nutrients to the soil, so the same materials can be used again. Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would not be recycled.

A food chain is a sequence showing who eats whom, through which energy and nutrients pass — for example, grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle. Each step is a trophic level. In nature, organisms usually eat more than one kind of food, so many food chains are linked together to form a food web.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three groups of biotic components of an ecosystem with one example of each.
examples.solution:
Biotic components are grouped by how they get food.

  • Producers — green plants.
  • Consumers — animals (e.g. deer, lion).
  • Decomposers — bacteria and fungi.
examples.answer: Producers (green plants), consumers (animals) and decomposers (bacteria and fungi).

examples.problem: Example 2: Why are decomposers important in an ecosystem?
examples.solution:
Decomposers recycle nutrients.

  • They break down dead organisms.
  • They return nutrients to the soil so producers can use them again, keeping nature's cycle going.
examples.answer: Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil, recycling materials for reuse by producers.

examples.problem: Example 3: In the food chain grass → deer → tiger, name the producer and the trophic level of the deer.
examples.solution:
The chain starts with the producer.

  • Producer: grass.
  • The deer eats the producer, so it is the primary consumer (first consumer level).
examples.answer: Grass is the producer; the deer is the primary consumer (a herbivore).

recap:
• An ecosystem has biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic (sunlight, water, air, soil) components.
  • Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) recycle nutrients from dead matter.
  • A food chain shows who eats whom (grass → grasshopper → frog → snake); each step is a trophic level.
  • Linked food chains form a food web.

quiz.q: Green plants in an ecosystem are called:
quiz.explanation: Green plants make their own food, so they are producers.

quiz.q: Bacteria and fungi that break down dead organisms are called:
quiz.explanation: Decomposers break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.

topics.title: Flow of Energy and Trophic Levels
topics.concept:
The energy that drives almost every ecosystem comes from the Sun. Producers (green plants) capture a small part of the Sun’s energy by photosynthesis and store it as chemical energy in food. This energy then flows from one trophic level to the next as one organism eats another.

An important feature of this energy flow is that it is one-way (unidirectional) — energy passes from the Sun to producers to consumers, and is lost as heat at each step; it does not flow back. At each step a lot of energy is used up by the organism for its life processes and lost to the surroundings as heat.

This gives the ten per cent law (given by Lindeman): on average, only about 10% of the energy available at one trophic level is passed on to the next; the other ~90% is lost. For example, if producers have 10,000 J of energy, herbivores get about 1000 J, the next carnivores about 100 J, and so on.

Because so much energy is lost at each step, food chains are usually short (rarely more than 4–5 levels) — there simply isn’t enough energy left to support many more levels. This is also why there are far fewer top carnivores than producers in an ecosystem.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is the flow of energy in an ecosystem said to be unidirectional?
examples.solution:
Energy moves in one direction only.

  • It flows from the Sun to producers to consumers.
  • At each step it is lost as heat and does not return to the previous level.
examples.answer: Because energy flows only from the Sun to producers to consumers and is lost as heat at each step, never flowing back.

examples.problem: Example 2: If producers in a food chain contain 20,000 J of energy, how much (approximately) reaches the primary consumers?
examples.solution:
Apply the ten per cent law.

  • Only about 10% passes to the next level.
  • 10% of 20,000 J = 2000 J.
examples.answer: About 2000 J (10% of 20,000 J) reaches the primary consumers.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why are food chains usually limited to only four or five trophic levels?
examples.solution:
Energy decreases sharply at each step.

  • About 90% of energy is lost at every level.
  • After a few levels too little energy is left to support another level.
examples.answer: Because about 90% of energy is lost at each step, so after four or five levels there is too little energy to support more.

recap:
• Energy flows from the Sun → producers → consumers; it is unidirectional and lost as heat at each step.
  • Ten per cent law: only ~10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.
  • Heavy energy loss keeps food chains short (4–5 levels) and top carnivores few.

quiz.q: According to the ten per cent law, the energy passed to the next trophic level is about:
quiz.explanation: Only about 10% of energy at one level passes to the next; the rest is lost.

quiz.q: The flow of energy in an ecosystem is:
quiz.explanation: Energy flows one way (Sun to producers to consumers) and is lost as heat.

topics.title: Environmental Problems: Ozone and Waste Management
topics.concept:
Human activity is harming the environment, and two important problems are ozone depletion and the growing amount of waste.

The ozone layer is a layer of ozone gas (O₃) high up in the atmosphere. It is very important because it absorbs the harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays of the Sun, which can cause skin cancer, eye damage and harm to crops and other living things. The ozone layer is being damaged (depleted) by man-made chemicals called CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons), once used in refrigerators, air conditioners and spray cans. To protect the ozone layer, the world agreed (in the Montreal Protocol) to stop making CFCs.

Waste management: the materials we throw away are of two kinds. Biodegradable wastes are broken down by decomposers (e.g. food scraps, paper, cotton, leaves). Non-biodegradable wastes are not broken down by natural processes and remain for a very long time (e.g. plastics, glass, metals, many chemicals); they pollute the land and water and harm living things. Managing waste involves: reducing the waste we produce, reusing items, recycling materials, and disposing of waste safely — including segregating (separating) biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste before disposal. Caring for the environment in these ways protects the ecosystems that all life depends on.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is the ozone layer important, and which chemicals damage it?
examples.solution:
Ozone shields us from UV rays.

  • It absorbs the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays, protecting living things.
  • It is damaged by CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons).
examples.answer: The ozone layer absorbs harmful UV rays; it is damaged by CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons).

examples.problem: Example 2: Classify as biodegradable or non-biodegradable: vegetable peels, plastic bottle, paper, glass.
examples.solution:
Biodegradable wastes are broken down by decomposers.

  • Biodegradable: vegetable peels, paper.
  • Non-biodegradable: plastic bottle, glass.
examples.answer: Biodegradable: vegetable peels and paper. Non-biodegradable: plastic bottle and glass.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why should biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes be separated (segregated) before disposal?
examples.solution:
The two need different handling.

  • Biodegradable waste can be composted or broken down naturally.
  • Non-biodegradable waste can be sent for recycling or safe disposal, instead of polluting.
examples.answer: So that biodegradable waste can be composted and non-biodegradable waste can be recycled or disposed of safely, reducing pollution.

recap:
• The ozone layer absorbs harmful UV rays; it is depleted by CFCs (banned by the Montreal Protocol).
  • Biodegradable wastes are broken down by decomposers (food, paper); non-biodegradable wastes are not (plastic, glass, metal).
  • Manage waste by reduce, reuse, recycle and segregating waste before disposal.

quiz.q: The ozone layer is important because it absorbs the Sun's harmful:
quiz.explanation: Ozone absorbs harmful UV rays that can cause skin cancer and other harm.

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-biodegradable waste?
quiz.explanation: Plastic is not broken down by natural processes, so it is non-biodegradable.

questions.q: A self-contained unit of living organisms interacting with their non-living surroundings is an:
questions.explanation: An ecosystem is the interacting unit of living and non-living components.

questions.q: Sunlight, water and soil in an ecosystem are its ___ components.
questions.explanation: Non-living physical factors are the abiotic components.

questions.q: Organisms that make their own food in an ecosystem are:
questions.explanation: Green plants are producers; they make their own food.

questions.q: Bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter are:
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down dead organisms and recycle nutrients.

questions.q: A sequence showing who eats whom, such as grass to deer to tiger, is a:
questions.explanation: A linear who-eats-whom sequence is a food chain.

questions.q: Each step in a food chain is called a:
questions.explanation: Each feeding step is a trophic level.

questions.q: Many interconnected food chains form a:
questions.explanation: Interlinked food chains make a food web.

questions.q: The ultimate source of energy for almost all ecosystems is the:
questions.explanation: The Sun's energy is captured by producers and flows through the ecosystem.

questions.q: The flow of energy through an ecosystem is:
questions.explanation: Energy flows one way and is lost as heat at each step.

questions.q: According to the ten per cent law, energy passed to the next trophic level is about:
questions.explanation: Only about 10% of energy moves to the next level; ~90% is lost.

questions.q: Food chains are usually short because:
options: Much energy is lost at each level
questions.explanation: Heavy energy loss at each level limits chains to 4-5 trophic levels.

questions.q: The ozone layer protects living things by absorbing harmful:
questions.explanation: Ozone absorbs the Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays.

questions.q: The ozone layer is damaged mainly by:
questions.explanation: CFCs are man-made chemicals that deplete the ozone layer.

questions.q: Which of these is a biodegradable waste?
questions.explanation: Vegetable peels are broken down by decomposers, so they are biodegradable.

questions.q: Separating biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes before disposal is called:
questions.explanation: Segregation separates wastes so each can be treated appropriately.

questions.q: If all the decomposers in an ecosystem suddenly disappeared, the most likely result would be:
options: Dead matter piles up and nutrients are not recycled
questions.explanation: Without decomposers, dead organisms accumulate and nutrients are not returned to the soil.

questions.q: In the chain grass (10,000 J) to deer to tiger, the tiger receives about:
questions.explanation: 10% to deer = 1000 J, then 10% to tiger = 100 J (ten per cent law applied twice).

questions.q: Harmful chemicals like pesticides become most concentrated in the bodies of top carnivores. This happens because:
options: The chemicals are passed up and build up along the food chain (biomagnification)
questions.explanation: Non-degradable chemicals accumulate at each level, becoming most concentrated at the top (biomagnification).

questions.q: Why is there usually a far smaller number of top carnivores than producers in an ecosystem?
options: Only a small fraction of energy reaches the top levels
questions.explanation: With ~90% energy lost per level, only a little energy reaches the top, supporting fewer organisms.

questions.q: A 'hole' in the ozone layer is a serious concern mainly because it lets in more:
questions.explanation: Less ozone means more harmful UV reaches the surface, increasing health and crop damage.

questions.q: Using cloth bags and composting kitchen waste at home helps the environment mainly by:
options: Reducing non-biodegradable waste and recycling nutrients
questions.explanation: It cuts plastic waste and returns biodegradable matter to the soil, aiding waste management.
